newsitem.title: GREECE: Governor of Black Sea bank hopes to open shop May.
newsitem.headline: Governor of Black Sea bank hopes to open shop May.

text.p: The Turkish governor of the new Black Sea economic cooperation bank, seen as the locomotive for the fledging group, said on Tuesday he hoped to start operations in this northern Greek city in May.

The long-delayed bank will be the financial backbone of the 11-nation Black Sea Economic Cooperation (BSEC) group, set up in 1993 to help build commercial ties among neighbours and traditional foes in the volatile region.

"All member countries have ratified the founding of the bank but some have not put up the money yet. I am hopeful that the depository issue will be resolved and the bank will begin operation in May," Governor Ersoy Volkan told Reuters.
A building, complete with a brass plaque, has long been provided by Greece but it remains empty until member states, some in desperate financial condition, cough up the cash.

Countries must contribute according to their share in the bank. Greece, Turkey and Russia have each been allocated 16.6 percent of shares, Bulgaria, Romania and Ukraine 13.5, while Albania, Georgia, Moldova, Armenia and Azerbaijan two percent.

The bank will start with an initial capital of one billion special drawing rights (SDRs) ($1.6 billion). SDRs are reserve assets created by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Their value is a composite of the dollar, yen, mark, pound and franc.
Greece, BSEC's only EU member has secured financial backing of Ecu 250,000 for an action plan for the pact but cannot use the money unless the bank opens.
Volkan, who has worked with Citibank in Ankara and New York and Eximbank Turkey, said he hoped to use his experience to raise funds from U.S. and Japanese financial institutions.
"We will have tough guidelines like the European Investment Bank and do serious work, otherwise it will be very difficult to raise funding," he said at a two-day Balkan economic conference.
Feuding neighbours Greece and Turkey agreed to locate the BSEC bank in Salonika provided its governor would be Turkish.
"It's not an easy job, I tell you," Volkan said. "But, although you can't totally separate it from politics, we must be professional and play an objective role."
